The article's focus on determining whether haptic slant adaptation is based on **proprioceptive posture** (unimanual) or **relative hand positions** (bimanual) is central to its experimental design. In **Experiment 3**, the researchers aimed to dissociate these two potential mechanisms by testing participants in conditions where **haptic feedback was absent** (Surface Absent condition) and where **only posture was involved**. 

To achieve this, they used the **Oculus Rift VR headset** equipped with **touch controllers**, which allowed them to **guide participants to specific hand positions without physical haptic feedback**. This setup enabled the researchers to **manipulate height differences** and **test whether adaptation persisted** in the absence of direct haptic input. The key insight from Experiment 3 is that **adaptation aftereffects still occurred even without haptic feedback**, supporting the idea that **proprioceptive posture**—not haptic cues—was the driving factor.

The **VR headset** was not primarily used to provide haptic feedback (as in the earlier experiments with PHANToM devices) but instead to **eliminate haptic feedback** and focus on the **role of posture**. This enabled the researchers to **distinguish between unimanual and bimanual adaptation mechanisms** by observing how changes in posture affected perceived slant. Thus, the **use of the VR headset in Experiment 3 was instrumental in exploring the conceptual distinction between relative static posture adaptation and low-level unimanual adaptation**, which aligns directly with **Option A**.
